learningObjectives.title: Emergence of authoritarian states (conditions and methods)

questions.q: Mussolini became Prime Minister of Italy in 1922 following the:
questions.explain: The threat of the Fascist 'March on Rome' led the king to appoint Mussolini PM in 1922.

questions.q: Hitler was appointed Chancellor of Germany in:
questions.explain: Hitler was legally appointed Chancellor in January 1933, then rapidly consolidated power.

questions.q: The Reichstag Fire (1933) was used by Hitler to:
options: Justify emergency powers and suppress the communists
questions.explain: The fire was used to pass the Reichstag Fire Decree, curbing civil liberties and targeting communists.

questions.q: The Enabling Act (1933) allowed Hitler to:
questions.explain: The Enabling Act let Hitler's government pass laws without parliamentary approval, a key step to dictatorship.

questions.q: Stalin emerged as leader of the USSR after Lenin's death mainly by:
options: Out-manoeuvring rivals such as Trotsky in a power struggle
A military coup against the Tsar
questions.explain: Stalin used his organisational position and alliances to defeat rivals like Trotsky in the 1920s power struggle.

questions.q: Stalin's Great Terror (1936-38) is characterised by:
options: Show trials and mass repression of perceived enemies
questions.explain: The Great Terror used purges, show trials and the NKVD to eliminate real and imagined opponents.

questions.q: Mao Zedong established the People's Republic of China in 1949 after victory in the:
options: Chinese Civil War against the Nationalists (GMD)
questions.explain: The CCP defeated Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists in the civil war, founding the PRC in 1949.

questions.q: A cult of personality and mass propaganda were used by authoritarian leaders to:
questions.explain: Propaganda and personality cults built loyalty and helped consolidate single-party rule.

questions.q: Stalin's Five-Year Plans were designed to:
questions.explain: The Five-Year Plans drove state-led heavy industrialisation from 1928.

questions.q: Collectivisation of agriculture in the USSR contributed to:
options: The end of the secret police
questions.explain: Forced collectivisation disrupted agriculture and caused famine (e.g. the Holodomor).

questions.q: Mao's Great Leap Forward (1958-62) resulted in:
options: Widespread famine and millions of deaths
questions.explain: The Great Leap Forward's agricultural and industrial policies caused catastrophic famine.

questions.q: The use of a secret police (e.g. the NKVD or Gestapo) is an example of maintaining power through:
questions.explain: Secret police enforced conformity and repressed opposition through surveillance and terror.

questions.q: Nazi economic policy in the 1930s included:
options: Rearmament and public works to reduce unemployment
Full free trade with all nations
Nationalising all farmland like the USSR
questions.explain: Rearmament and schemes like autobahn construction cut unemployment and prepared for war.

questions.q: A common condition that helped authoritarian leaders gain power was:
questions.explain: Economic hardship and weak institutions (e.g. post-WWI, the Depression) enabled extremist movements.

questions.q: The Night of the Long Knives (1934) saw Hitler eliminate:
options: The SA leadership and other rivals
questions.explain: Hitler purged Ernst Röhm and the SA leadership, securing army support and his own dominance.

questions.q: Nazi social policy towards women emphasised roles summarised as:
questions.explain: Nazi ideology promoted a domestic role for women focused on family and motherhood.

questions.q: Mussolini's 'Battle for Grain' aimed to:
questions.explain: The Battle for Grain sought agricultural self-sufficiency (autarky) for Fascist Italy.

questions.q: Legal methods used by Hitler to gain power (e.g. the Enabling Act) show that authoritarian regimes could rise:
options: Partly through existing legal and constitutional means
Only by winning free elections outright
questions.explain: Hitler combined legal manoeuvres with intimidation, rather than a single violent seizure.

questions.q: Historians who debate whether Hitler was a 'weak dictator' or fully in control are engaging in:
questions.explain: The 'intentionalist vs structuralist' debate is an example of differing historiographical interpretations.

questions.q: A leader who uses propaganda, a secret police and a state-directed economy while banning other parties is best described as:
questions.explain: These combined methods of persuasion, force and control characterise single-party authoritarian rule.
